title: No scorekeeping
hookLine: only those who place good in the will can truly be friends (Discourses 2.22)

cards: Two puppies are tumbling around on the rug, licking each other's faces, best friends. Now drop a piece of meat between them. In about half a second you'll see what the friendship was made of.
The licking stops. The growling starts. Whatever the friendship was, it didn't survive one piece of meat.
Epictetus used exactly that picture, and then he dropped other things between people: a piece of land, a throne.

teach.h: WE LOVE WHAT WE THINK IS GOOD.
teach.b: This is Discourses book two, chapter twenty-two, on friendship. Epictetus starts with a simple claim: we love what we think is good. So who can really be a friend?
Only someone who knows what's actually good. Then the dogs: throw meat between them and you'll see. Then people.
Throw a field between a father and a son, and see how fast the son wants his father gone, and the father the son.
He reaches for an old story: Eteocles and Polynices, two brothers in Greek legend who fought over the throne of Thebes and, as the legend tells it, killed each other.
They'd been raised together, eaten and drunk together, slept under one roof. The throne fell between them like the meat.

His diagnosis: wherever a person puts their I and their mine, that's where they lean. If my good is in money, your money is always a little bit against me. If my good is in being admired, your success is a threat.
That's when friends start keeping score: who called whom, who paid last, who got the better job.
But if my good is in my own will, in being honest and kind and faithful, nothing that falls between us can turn you into a rival. You can't steal my honesty by getting the promotion.
That, Epictetus says, is the only ground a lasting friendship can stand on: two people who've placed their good where no piece of meat can land.

how: Some readers of this chapter check their friendships for a hidden ledger, and practice acts of friendship with nothing expected back.

o: friendship with no tally, since your good lies within
a game played for fun, with no points counted
a rule never to lend money to a friend

p: drop meat between them and see
a friend's gain feels like your loss

s: Epictetus says anyone can be a true friend, whatever they value
only someone who places their good in the will, where nothing can fall between friends.
he uses dogs fighting over meat as a picture of failed friendship
and then a field dropped between a father and a son.
Eteocles and Polynices shared the throne of Thebes peacefully
in the legend the two brothers killed each other over it.

games.q: two old friends are up for the same promotion. according to Epictetus, what decides whether the friendship survives?
o: where each of them places their good.
games.why: if their good is in the job, the friendship becomes a contest; if it's in their own character, the promotion can't make them rivals.

practice: Bring to mind a friend, a sibling or a partner, and notice if a quiet ledger is running: who reached out last, who gave more, who owes whom. No scolding; just see it.
Then, for a few breaths, set the ledger down, and picture one kind thing done for them with no entry made and nothing expected back.

wordCard.voice: No scorekeeping. Epictetus on friendship: when your good lies in your own character, nothing that falls between friends can make them rivals.

orig.note: Greek philia: friendship, affection; the subject of Discourses 2.22.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing to keep score of. Good placed in the will can't land between friends. See you tomorrow.
